claim: Hemocytes in the caterpillar Pieris rapae are able to synthesize 5-HT following activation by lipopolysaccharide.
source: We report that hemocytes in the caterpillar, Pieris rapae are able to synthesize 5-HT following activation by lipopolysaccharide.
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling, fluorescence microscopy, RT-PCR, ELISA, and real-time quantitative RT-PCR data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Inhibition of a serotonin-generating enzyme with pharmacological blockade impaired hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: The inhibition of a serotonin-generating enzyme with either pharmacological blockade or RNAi knock-down impaired hemocyte phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that AMTP treatment and siTPH treatment reduced phagocytosis, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inhibition of a serotonin-generating enzyme with RNAi knock-down impaired hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: The inhibition of a serotonin-generating enzyme with either pharmacological blockade or RNAi knock-down impaired hemocyte phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that siTPH treatment reduced phagocytosis, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Naive hemocytes primarily express 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors.
source: Biochemical and functional experiments showed that naive hemocytes primarily express 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR, immunofluorescence, and Ca2+ imaging data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Blockade of 5-HT1B significantly reduced phagocytic ability.
source: The blockade of 5-HT1B significantly reduced phagocytic ability; however, the blockade of 5-HT2B increased hemocyte phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological blockade experiments and RNAi experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Blockade of 5-HT2B increased hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: The blockade of 5-HT1B significantly reduced phagocytic ability; however, the blockade of 5-HT2B increased hemocyte phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological blockade experiments and RNAi experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: 5-HT1B-null Drosophila melanogaster mutants showed higher mortality than controls when infected with bacteria.
source: The 5-HT1B-null Drosophila melanogaster mutants showed higher mortality than controls when infected with bacteria, due to their decreased phagocytotic ability.
evidence: Supported by survival curve data and bacterial load measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: 5-HT1B-null Drosophila melanogaster mutants showed decreased phagocytotic ability.
source: The 5-HT1B-null Drosophila melanogaster mutants showed higher mortality than controls when infected with bacteria, due to their decreased phagocytotic ability.
evidence: Supported by in vivo phagocytosis assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Flies expressing 5-HT1B RNAi in hemocytes showed sensitivity to infection.
source: Flies expressing 5-HT1B or 5-HT2B RNAi in hemocytes also showed similar sensitivity to infection.
evidence: Supported by survival curves and bacterial load data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Flies expressing 5-HT2B RNAi in hemocytes showed sensitivity to infection.
source: Flies expressing 5-HT1B or 5-HT2B RNAi in hemocytes also showed similar sensitivity to infection.
evidence: Supported by survival curves and bacterial load data shown in Figure 8.

claim: 5-HT mediates hemocyte phagocytosis through 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors.
source: Combined, these data demonstrate that 5-HT mediates hemocyte phagocytosis through 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors and serotonergic signaling performs critical modulatory functions in immune systems of animals separated by 500 million years of evolution.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches including pharmacological blockade, RNAi, and genetic mutants across Figures 2-8.

claim: Serotonergic signaling performs critical modulatory functions in immune systems of animals separated by 500 million years of evolution.
source: Combined, these data demonstrate that 5-HT mediates hemocyte phagocytosis through 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors and serotonergic signaling performs critical modulatory functions in immune systems of animals separated by 500 million years of evolution.
evidence: Inferred from the conservation of serotonergic immune modulation observed in both insects (P. rapae and D. melanogaster) and vertebrates as discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: Serotonin is one of the oldest neurotransmitters/hormones in evolution.
source: Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) is one of the oldest neurotransmitters/hormones in evolution (Turlejski, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Turlejski, 1996.

claim: 5-HT regulates or modulates metabolism in nematodes.
source: It regulates or modulates a wide variety of processes in most invertebrates and vertebrates, such as metabolism (Sze et al., 2000) and locomotion (Ranganathan et al., 2000) in nematodes; reproduction (Anstey et al., 2009), learning and memory (Sitaraman et al., 2008) in insects; physiologic states and behaviors, including pain, appetite, mood, and sleep (Mössner and Lesch, 1998) in humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sze et al., 2000.

claim: 5-HT regulates or modulates locomotion in nematodes.
source: It regulates or modulates a wide variety of processes in most invertebrates and vertebrates, such as metabolism (Sze et al., 2000) and locomotion (Ranganathan et al., 2000) in nematodes; reproduction (Anstey et al., 2009), learning and memory (Sitaraman et al., 2008) in insects; physiologic states and behaviors, including pain, appetite, mood, and sleep (Mössner and Lesch, 1998) in humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ranganathan et al., 2000.

claim: 5-HT regulates or modulates reproduction in insects.
source: It regulates or modulates a wide variety of processes in most invertebrates and vertebrates, such as metabolism (Sze et al., 2000) and locomotion (Ranganathan et al., 2000) in nematodes; reproduction (Anstey et al., 2009), learning and memory (Sitaraman et al., 2008) in insects; physiologic states and behaviors, including pain, appetite, mood, and sleep (Mössner and Lesch, 1998) in humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Anstey et al., 2009.

claim: 5-HT regulates or modulates learning and memory in insects.
source: It regulates or modulates a wide variety of processes in most invertebrates and vertebrates, such as metabolism (Sze et al., 2000) and locomotion (Ranganathan et al., 2000) in nematodes; reproduction (Anstey et al., 2009), learning and memory (Sitaraman et al., 2008) in insects; physiologic states and behaviors, including pain, appetite, mood, and sleep (Mössner and Lesch, 1998) in humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sitaraman et al., 2008.

claim: 5-HT regulates or modulates pain, appetite, mood, and sleep in humans.
source: It regulates or modulates a wide variety of processes in most invertebrates and vertebrates, such as metabolism (Sze et al., 2000) and locomotion (Ranganathan et al., 2000) in nematodes; reproduction (Anstey et al., 2009), learning and memory (Sitaraman et al., 2008) in insects; physiologic states and behaviors, including pain, appetite, mood, and sleep (Mössner and Lesch, 1998) in humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mössner and Lesch, 1998.

claim: 5-HT plays an important role outside of the central nervous system in immune signaling.
source: 5-HT also plays an important role outside of the central nervous system (CNS) in immune signaling.
evidence: Supported by subsequent discussion of immune cell expression of 5-HT synthesizing enzymes and receptors.

claim: Immune cells can synthesize and sequester 5-HT.
source: Immune cells can synthesize and sequester 5-HT.
evidence: Supported by examples of human mast cells and mouse dendritic cells cited in the text.

claim: Human mast cells express the key peripheral 5-HT synthesizing enzyme, tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH-1).
source: For instance, human mast cells express the key peripheral 5-HT synthesizing enzyme, tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH-1) (Kushnir-Sukhov et al., 2007, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kushnir-Sukhov et al., 2007, 2008.

claim: Mouse dendritic cells express the serotonin transporter (SERT), taking up 5-HT from the microenvironment.
source: Mouse dendritic cells (DCs) express the serotonin transporter (SERT), taking up 5-HT from the microenvironment (O'Connell et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Connell et al., 2006.

claim: 5-HT regulates immune responses and inflammatory cascades via distinct receptors.
source: 5-HT regulates immune responses and inflammatory cascades via distinct receptors and different immune cells have been shown to express a different composition of 5-HT receptor subtypes (Baganz and Blakely, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baganz and Blakely, 2013.

claim: Different immune cells have been shown to express a different composition of 5-HT receptor subtypes.
source: 5-HT regulates immune responses and inflammatory cascades via distinct receptors and different immune cells have been shown to express a different composition of 5-HT receptor subtypes (Baganz and Blakely, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baganz and Blakely, 2013.

claim: 5-HT2A may contribute to chemotaxis of eosinophils.
source: 5-HT2A may contribute to chemotaxis of eosinophils (Boehme et al., 2008) and 5-HT2C receptors on alveolar macrophages can be activated by 5-HT (Mikulski et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boehme et al., 2008.

claim: 5-HT2C receptors on alveolar macrophages can be activated by 5-HT.
source: 5-HT2A may contribute to chemotaxis of eosinophils (Boehme et al., 2008) and 5-HT2C receptors on alveolar macrophages can be activated by 5-HT (Mikulski et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mikulski et al., 2010.

claim: The function of 5-HT signaling in vivo in immune responses are still unclear.
source: However, most studies assess the in vitro response of immune cells to pharmacological agents. Therefore, the function of 5-HT signaling in vivo in are still unclear.
evidence: Based on the observation that most studies are in vitro.

claim: Phagocytosis is a highly conserved aspect of innate immunity.
source: Vertebrate blood cells (e.g. macrophages) have evolved a variety of strategies to internalize particles and solutes, including pinocytosis, receptor-mediated endocytosis, and phagocytosis, a highly conserved aspect of innate immunity.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about innate immunity.

claim: Phagocytosis is the uptake of large particles (>0.5 μm) into cells.
source: Phagocytosis, the uptake of large particles (>0.5 μm) into cells, allows for rapid engulfment of dying cells and pathogens by specialized phagocytes, such as macrophages and neutrophils in mammals (Aderem and Underhill, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aderem and Underhill, 1999.

claim: Phagocytosis allows for rapid engulfment of dying cells and pathogens by specialized phagocytes, such as macrophages and neutrophils in mammals.
source: Phagocytosis, the uptake of large particles (>0.5 μm) into cells, allows for rapid engulfment of dying cells and pathogens by specialized phagocytes, such as macrophages and neutrophils in mammals (Aderem and Underhill, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aderem and Underhill, 1999.

claim: In insects, hemocyte phagocytosis is an important cellular defense response to pathogens and parasites.
source: In insects, hemocyte phagocytosis is an important cellular defense response to pathogens and parasites (Lavine and Strand, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lavine and Strand, 2002.

claim: In lepidopteran insects, the granulocytes and plasmatocytes are the major phagocytes.
source: In lepidopteran insects, the granulocytes and plasmatocytes are the major phagocytes (Kanost et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanost et al., 2004.

claim: There is evidence that 5-HT can enhance phagocytosis.
source: However, the roles of serotonin in insect phagocytosis are less well characterized compared with vertebrate counterparts, although there is evidence that 5-HT can enhance phagocytosis (Baines et al., 1992; Kim et al.,2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baines et al., 1992 and Kim et al., 2009.

claim: Many of the intracellular signaling pathways that drive the insect immune system are very similar to those found in the mammalian innate immune system.
source: Many of the intracellular signaling pathways that drive the insect immune system are very similar to those found in the mammalian innate immune system (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007), and some of them were first uncovered in insects (Hoffmann, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007 and Hoffmann, 2003.

claim: Some intracellular signaling pathways in the mammalian innate immune system were first uncovered in insects.
source: Many of the intracellular signaling pathways that drive the insect immune system are very similar to those found in the mammalian innate immune system (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007), and some of them were first uncovered in insects (Hoffmann, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoffmann, 2003.

claim: Indirect evidence suggests that similarities between insects and mammals extend to the molecular mechanisms involved in the neuroendocrine control of immune function.
source: Indirect evidence suggests that similarities between insects and mammals extend to the molecular mechanisms involved in the neuroendocrine control of immune function (Adamo, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adamo, 2008.

claim: Hemocyte-derived 5-HT regulates phagocytosis in an autocrine manner through 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors.
source: We found that hemocyte-derived 5-HT regulates phagocytosis in an autocrine manner through 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors, each of which produces distinct effects.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing hemocyte synthesis of 5-HT and receptor-mediated effects on phagocytosis.

claim: 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B produce distinct effects on phagocytosis.
source: We found that hemocyte-derived 5-HT regulates phagocytosis in an autocrine manner through 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors, each of which produces distinct effects.
evidence: Supported by data showing opposite effects of 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B blockade on phagocytosis in P. rapae.

claim: Both 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B are necessary for effective resistance to bacterial infections.
source: Mortality experiments using Drosophila mutants and hemocyte-specific RNAi-silencing further found that both 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B are necessary for effective resistance to bacterial infections.
evidence: Supported by survival and bacterial load data from Drosophila experiments in Figures 6-8.

claim: After activation with 100 ng/ml of lipopolysaccharide for 2 hr, 5-HT was detected within hemocytes by immunolabeling and fluorescence microscopy.
source: After activation with 100 ng/ml of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) for 2 hr, we detected 5-HT within hemocytes directly by immunolabeling and fluorescence microscopy.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Granules of 5-HT labeled with 5-HT antisera are readily visible in the cytosol of LPS-activated hemocytes.
source: Figure 1A shows that granules of 5-HT labeled with 5-HT antisera (upper) are readily visible in the cytosol.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A showing immunofluorescence staining.

claim: Serotonin synthesis requires two enzymes, tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC).
source: Serotonin synthesis requires two enzymes, tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge of serotonin biosynthesis pathway shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tryptophan hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in serotonin biosynthesis.
source: Tryptophan hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in serotonin biosynthesis encoded by two genes, TPH and TRH in insects, TPH1 and TPH2 in mammals.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Tryptophan hydroxylase is encoded by two genes, TPH and TRH in insects, TPH1 and TPH2 in mammals.
source: Tryptophan hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in serotonin biosynthesis encoded by two genes, TPH and TRH in insects, TPH1 and TPH2 in mammals.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of gene nomenclature across species.

claim: Both TPH and TRH gene products have tryptophan hydroxylase activity in vivo.
source: Both gene products have tryptophan hydroxylase activity in vivo.
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: The TPH/TPH1 gene is expressed in non-neural tissues.
source: The TPH/TPH1 gene is expressed in non-neural tissues, and the TRH/TPH2 gene is expressed in neural tissues (Côté et al., 2003; Neckameyer et al., 2007; Watanabe et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Côté et al., 2003; Neckameyer et al., 2007; Watanabe et al., 2011.

claim: The TRH/TPH2 gene is expressed in neural tissues.
source: The TPH/TPH1 gene is expressed in non-neural tissues, and the TRH/TPH2 gene is expressed in neural tissues (Côté et al., 2003; Neckameyer et al., 2007; Watanabe et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Côté et al., 2003; Neckameyer et al., 2007; Watanabe et al., 2011.

claim: The high-affinity SERT is a plasma membrane protein that can take up extracellular 5-HT.
source: The high-affinity SERT is a plasma membrane protein that can take up extracellular 5-HT (Rudnick, 2006; Torres et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rudnick, 2006 and Torres et al., 2003.

claim: Hemocytes produced mRNA for TPH.
source: Figure 1C shows that hemocytes produced mRNA for TPH, but that transcripts of TRH and SERT were not detected.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Transcripts of TRH and SERT were not detected in hemocytes.
source: Figure 1C shows that hemocytes produced mRNA for TPH, but that transcripts of TRH and SERT were not detected.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Hemocytes do not selectively sequester 5-HT but can synthesize 5-HT using TPH.
source: These results suggest that hemocytes do not selectively sequester 5-HT but can synthesize 5-HT using TPH.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of SERT expression and presence of TPH expression in hemocytes.

claim: 5-HT levels increased significantly above controls in cell supernatants 1 hr after exposure of hemocytes to LPS.
source: 5-HT levels increased significantly above that found in controls in cell supernatants 1 hr after exposure of hemocytes to LPS.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 5-HT levels reached maximal at 2 hr after LPS exposure.
source: 5-HT levels reached maximal at 2 hr and decreased at 4 hr (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 5-HT levels decreased at 4 hr after LPS exposure.
source: 5-HT levels reached maximal at 2 hr and decreased at 4 hr (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: mRNA expression level of TPH was up-regulated by approximately sixfold relative to controls at 15 min after LPS stimulation.
source: The real-time quantitative RT-PCR results also show that mRNA expression level of TPH was up-regulated by approximately sixfold relative to controls at 15 min and at 4 hr after LPS stimulation, suggesting a potential negative feedback regulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by real-time quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: mRNA expression level of TPH was up-regulated by approximately sixfold relative to controls at 4 hr after LPS stimulation.
source: The real-time quantitative RT-PCR results also show that mRNA expression level of TPH was up-regulated by approximately sixfold relative to controls at 15 min and at 4 hr after LPS stimulation, suggesting a potential negative feedback regulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by real-time quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The pattern of TPH expression suggests a potential negative feedback regulation.
source: The real-time quantitative RT-PCR results also show that mRNA expression level of TPH was up-regulated by approximately sixfold relative to controls at 15 min and at 4 hr after LPS stimulation, suggesting a potential negative feedback regulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Inferred from the temporal pattern of TPH expression shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Hemocytes are able to synthesize and release 5-HT in vitro.
source: Therefore, it is concluded that hemocytes are able to synthesize and release 5-HT in vitro, and this activity is enhanced following their activation.
evidence: Supported by ELISA and RT-PCR data in Figure 1.

claim: Hemocyte synthesis and release of 5-HT is enhanced following their activation.
source: Therefore, it is concluded that hemocytes are able to synthesize and release 5-HT in vitro, and this activity is enhanced following their activation.
evidence: Supported by time-course data showing increased 5-HT and TPH expression after LPS stimulation in Figure 1.

claim: α-methyltryptophan (AMTP) is a competitive inhibitor of 5-HT synthesis.
source: α-methyltryptophan (AMTP) is a competitive inhibitor of 5-HT synthesis (Gal and Christiansen, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gal and Christiansen, 1975.

claim: 5-HT synthesis was significantly reduced in hemocytes after treatment with 10 μM AMTP, compared with PBS-treated controls.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, 5-HT synthesis was significantly reduced in hemocytes after treatment with 10 μM AMTP, compared with PBS-treated controls.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 10 μM AMTP significantly impaired hemocyte phagocytic ability.
source: The results show that 10 μM AMTP also significantly impaired hemocyte phagocytic ability.
evidence: Supported by phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Treatment with exogenous 5-HT at 100 nM fully restored hemocyte phagocytosis after AMTP treatment.
source: Furthermore, treatment with exogenous 5-HT at 100 nM fully restored hemocyte phagocytosis (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: siTPH treatment achieved approximately 80% knock-down effect.
source: Next, we tested siTPH-treated hemocytes (knock-down effect was approximately 80%, Figure 2E) for their phagocytosis ability.
evidence: Supported by real-time qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: After incubation with siTPH for 48 hr, hemocyte phagocytosis rate was significantly decreased compared with the negative control.
source: After incubation with siTPH for 48 hr, hemocyte phagocytosis rate was significantly decreased compared with the negative control.
evidence: Supported by phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: 100 nM 5-HT treatment could fully rescue the siTPH induced phenotype.
source: 100 nM 5-HT treatment could fully rescue the siTPH induced phenotype (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: Supported by phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: Hemocyte-derived 5-HT is critical for proper hemocyte phagocytosis upon immune challenge.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that hemocyte-derived 5-HT is critical for proper hemocyte phagocytosis upon immune challenge.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of AMTP and siTPH experiments showing impaired phagocytosis and rescue by exogenous 5-HT.

claim: Five subtypes of 5-HT receptors including 5-HT1A, 5-HT1B, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B and 5-HT7 are identified in insects.
source: So far, five subtypes of 5-HT receptors including 5-HT1A, 5-HT1B, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B and 5-HT7 are identified in insects (Blenau and Thamm, 2011; Gasque et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blenau and Thamm, 2011 and Gasque et al., 2013.

claim: 5-HT1A and 5-HT1B couple with Gi protein and decrease intracellular cAMP levels.
source: 5-HT1A and 5-HT1B couple with Gi protein and decrease intracellular cAMP levels.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of G-protein coupled receptor signaling, supported by citations to Blenau and Thamm, 2011 and Gasque et al., 2013.

claim: 5-HT2A and 5-HT2B couple with Gq protein, which can induce increased intracellular Ca2+.
source: 5-HT2A and 5-HT2B couple with Gq protein, which can induce increased intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of G-protein coupled receptor signaling, supported by citations to Blenau and Thamm, 2011 and Gasque et al., 2013.

claim: 5-HT7 couples with Gs protein and increases cAMP levels.
source: 5-HT7 couples with Gs protein and increases cAMP levels (Blenau and Thamm, 2011; Gasque et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blenau and Thamm, 2011 and Gasque et al., 2013.

claim: Naive hemocytes express Pr5-HT1B, Pr5-HT2B and Pr5-HT7.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, naive hemocytes express Pr5-HT1B, Pr5-HT2B and Pr5-HT7.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Pr5-HT1B is expressed on the plasma membranes of hemocytes.
source: We used specific antibodies to confirm the expression of Pr5-HT1B (Figure 3B) and Pr5-HT2B (Figure 3C) on the plasma membranes of hemocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pr5-HT2B is expressed on the plasma membranes of hemocytes.
source: We used specific antibodies to confirm the expression of Pr5-HT1B (Figure 3B) and Pr5-HT2B (Figure 3C) on the plasma membranes of hemocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both plasmatocytes and granulocytes produced intracellular Ca2+ increase in response to 5-HT.
source: Both plasmatocytes and granulocytes, the two most abundant types of hemocytes, produced intracellular Ca2+ increase in response to 5-HT.
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 5-HT stimulated Ca2+ responses at concentrations ranging from 0.01 nM to 10 nM (maximal response).
source: 5-HT stimulated Ca2+ responses at concentrations ranging from 0.01 nM to 10 nM (maximal response), and its EC50 value was estimated at 0.15 nM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging dose-response data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The EC50 value of 5-HT for Ca2+ responses in hemocytes was estimated at 0.15 nM.
source: 5-HT stimulated Ca2+ responses at concentrations ranging from 0.01 nM to 10 nM (maximal response), and its EC50 value was estimated at 0.15 nM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging dose-response data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only blockade of Pr5-HT1B significantly reduced the phagocytic ability of hemocytes.
source: We found that only blockade of Pr5-HT1B significantly reduced the phagocytic ability of hemocytes.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological blockade experiments shown in Figure 3D-H.

claim: Blockade of Pr5-HT7 neither intensified nor reduced hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: Blockade of Pr5-HT7 neither intensified nor reduced hemocyte phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological blockade experiments shown in Figure 3D-H.

claim: Blockade of 5-HT2B significantly increased hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: Surprisingly, blockade of 5-HT2B significantly increased hemocyte phagocytosis (Figure 3D–H).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological blockade experiments shown in Figure 3D-H.

claim: The 5-HT1B blocker SB 216641 affected hemocyte phagocytosis in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We further found that the 5-HT1B blocker SB 216641 affected hemocyte phagocytosis in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: siPr5-HT1B decreased Pr5-HT1B expression significantly at both mRNA and protein levels.
source: The results showed that siPr5-HT1Bdecreased Pr5-HT1B expression significantly at both mRNA and protein levels (Figures 4B–C) after 24 hr and 48 hr, respectively.
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR and Western blot data shown in Figures 4B-C.

claim: siPr5-HT1B treated hemocytes phagocytose E. coli poorly compared with control.
source: As expected, the siPr5-HT1B treated hemocytes phagocytose E. coli poorly compared with control (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Knock-down of Pr5-HT2B was observed at both transcript and protein levels at 48 hr.
source: Significantly knock-down of Pr5-HT2B was also observed at both transcript and protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B) at 48 hr, which promoted hemocyte phagocytosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Knock-down of Pr5-HT2B promoted hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: Significantly knock-down of Pr5-HT2B was also observed at both transcript and protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B) at 48 hr, which promoted hemocyte phagocytosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Knock-down of Pr5-HT7 have no significant effect on hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: However, knock-down of Pr5-HT7have no significant effect on hemocyte phagocytosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Supported by phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: 5-HT mediates hemocyte phagocytosis through 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors but these two receptors act in opposite ways.
source: The results demonstrate that 5-HT mediates hemocyte phagocytosis through 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors but that these two receptors act in opposite ways.
evidence: Inferred from the combined pharmacological and RNAi data showing opposite effects of 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B on phagocytosis.

claim: Enhanced hemocyte phagocytosis is the overall effect by hemocytes exposed to released 5-HT.
source: Although the above data showed that activation of Pr5-HT1B and Pr5-HT2B produced opposite effects, enhanced hemocyte phagocytosis is the overall effect by hemocytes exposed to released 5-HT.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that exogenous 5-HT enhances phagocytosis despite opposite receptor effects.

claim: The mRNA levels of Pr5-HT1B was significantly increased after LPS stimulation from 15 min to 4 hr.
source: qPCR results showed that the mRNA levels of Pr5-HT1B was significantly increased after LPS stimulation from 15 min to 4 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The protein expression levels of Pr5-HT1B increased at 2 hr and 4 hr after LPS stimulation.
source: The protein expression levels also increased at 2 hr and 4 hr (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The mRNA expression level of Pr5-HT2B was significantly decreased after LPS induction at 1 hr and 4 hr.
source: Interestingly, the mRNA expression level of Pr5-HT2B was significantly decreased after LPS induction at 1 hr and 4 hr (Figure 5B), in accordance with its protein expression levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The protein expression level of Pr5-HT2B decreased after LPS induction in accordance with its mRNA levels.
source: Interestingly, the mRNA expression level of Pr5-HT2B was significantly decreased after LPS induction at 1 hr and 4 hr (Figure 5B), in accordance with its protein expression levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Both 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B transcripts were detected in wild-type Drosophila hemocytes by RT-PCR.
source: Both 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B transcripts were detected in wild-type Drosophila hemocytes by RT-PCR.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: High mRNA levels of Henna, the Drosophila TPH homolog, were expressed in hemocytes.
source: High mRNA levels of Henna, the Drosophila TPH homolog, were also expressed in hemocytes (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A 1344 bp fragment is removed from genomic DNA to disrupt the III-V transmembrane domains of the 5-HT1BΔIII-V allele.
source: A 1344 bp fragment is removed from genomic DNA to disrupt the III-V transmembrane domains of the 5-HT1BΔIII-V allele (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by genomic PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In 5-HT1BΔIII-V flies, in vivo phagocytosis of E. coli was strongly impaired when compared to controls.
source: In 5-HT1BΔIII-V flies, in vivo phagocytosis of E. coli was strongly impaired when compared to controls (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: A similar effect on phagocytosis was observed with the Gram-positive bacterium S. aureus in 5-HT1BΔIII-V flies.
source: A similar effect was observed with the Gram-positive bacterium S. aureus (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Supported by in vivo phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: After infection with S. aureus, 5-HT1BΔIII-V flies die more quickly than controls, for both male and female flies.
source: After infection with S. aureus, 5-HT1BΔIII-V flies die more quickly than controls, for both male and female flies (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: There is an increased bacterial load in 5-HT1B null flies compared to control files.
source: There is an increased bacterial load in 5-HT1B null flies compared to control files (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: HmlΔ-Gal4 driver was used to specifically express UAS-1B RNAi and UAS-5-HT1B RNAi25833, both of which led to decreased phagocytosis of E. coli and S. aureus.
source: We used the HmlΔ-Gal4 (Sinenko et al., 2004) driver to specifically express UAS-1B RNAi (Yuan et al. 2005) and UAS-5-HT1B RNAi25833 respectively, both of which led to decreased phagocytosis of E. coli and S. aureus (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: When flies were injected with 5-HT, knocking down 5-HT1B failed to enhance latex beads phagocytosis as controls.
source: However, when flies were injected with 5-HT, knocking down 5-HT1B failed to enhance latex beads phagocytosis as controls (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by latex bead phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: After injection with S. aureus, the flies expressing 5-HT1B RNAi in their blood cells were much weaker than the control flies.
source: After injection with S. aureus, the flies expressing 5-HT1B RNAi in their blood cells were much weaker than the control flies (Figure 7F–I).
evidence: Supported by survival curve and bacterial load data shown in Figure 7F-I.

claim: The increased susceptibility to bacteria in 5-HT1B mutants is due to 5-HT1B malfunction in hemocytes.
source: Our RNAi data indicate that the increased susceptibility to bacteria in 5-HT1B mutants is due to 5-HT1B malfunction in hemocytes.
evidence: Inferred from hemocyte-specific RNAi experiments showing similar phenotypes to null mutants.

claim: The reduced levels of 5-HT2B in Drosophila hemocytes led to a defect in the phagocytosis of E. coli and S. aureus.
source: Unlike the results found in P. rapae, the reduced levels of 5-HT2B in Drosophila hemocytes led to a defect in the phagocytosis of E. coli and S. aureus (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: The flies expressing 5-HT2B RNAi in their hemocytes took up significantly fewer latex beads than did control flies after 5-HT injection.
source: Moreover, the flies expressing 5-HT2B RNAi in their hemocytes took up significantly fewer latex beads than did control flies after 5-HT injection (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by latex bead phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: 5-HT2B knockdown flies had higher bacterial loads than controls.
source: 5-HT2B knockdown flies had higher bacterial loads than controls (Figure 8I) and increased susceptibility to S. aureus (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 8I.

claim: 5-HT2B knockdown flies had increased susceptibility to S. aureus.
source: 5-HT2B knockdown flies had higher bacterial loads than controls (Figure 8I) and increased susceptibility to S. aureus (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 8E-G.

claim: Both 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B play important roles in host defense against bacterial infection.
source: Taken together, our experiments demonstrate that both 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B play important roles in host defense against bacterial infection.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of mutant and RNAi experiments showing increased susceptibility to infection.

claim: Insect hemocytes express TPH and can synthesize 5-HT, like human macrophages.
source: This paper is the first to demonstrate that insect hemocytes express TPH and can synthesize 5-HT, like human macrophages (Nakamura et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and citation to Nakamura et al., 2008.

claim: The exposure of hemocytes to LPS led to an induction of TPH expression and a release of 5-HT.
source: The exposure of hemocytes to LPS led to an induction of TPH expression and a release of 5-HT.
evidence: Supported by ELISA and qPCR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The secreted 5-HT appears to be an important autocrine stimulus.
source: Moreover, the secreted 5-HT appears to be an important autocrine stimulus.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hemocytes synthesize and respond to 5-HT.

claim: 5-HT promotes phagocytosis.
source: It promotes phagocytosis: inhibition of TPH either by a competitive inhibitor or siRNA silencing resulted in significantly decreased hemocyte phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that inhibition of 5-HT synthesis reduces phagocytosis.

claim: Chemicals that act as neurotransmitters in the nervous system can also modulate immune function.
source: Chemicals that act as neurotransmitters in the nervous system can also modulate immune function (Meredith et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meredith et al., 2005.

claim: 5-HT is one of the classical neurotransmitters that is also an important immune regulatory molecule in both insects and mammals.
source: 5-HT is one of these classical neurotransmitters that is also an important immune regulatory molecule in both insects and mammals.
evidence: Based on the experimental findings in this study and cited literature.

claim: 5-HT was reported to mediate immune responses, such as hemocyte phagocytosis, nodule formation and hemocyte population in insects.
source: 5-HT was also reported to mediate immune responses, such as hemocyte phagocytosis, nodule formation and hemocyte population in insects (Baines et al., 1992; Kim et al., 2009; Kim and Kim, 2010), but the signaling pathway is unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Baines et al., 1992; Kim et al., 2009; Kim and Kim, 2010.

claim: The signaling pathway by which 5-HT mediates immune responses in insects is unclear.
source: 5-HT was also reported to mediate immune responses, such as hemocyte phagocytosis, nodule formation and hemocyte population in insects (Baines et al., 1992; Kim et al., 2009; Kim and Kim, 2010), but the signaling pathway is unclear.
evidence: Based on the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Drosophila TPH homolog gene Henna was found to be one hit in a genome-wide RNAi screen for genes that affect phagocytosis of Candida albicans by hemocytes.
source: Drosophila TPH homolog gene Henna was found to be one hit in a genome-wide RNAi screen for genes that affect phagocytosis of Candida albicans by hemocytes (Stroschein-Stevenson et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stroschein-Stevenson et al., 2006.

claim: Examining the basic interactions between serotonin receptor-medicated second messenger systems and immune-related intracellular signaling pathways may be easier in insects.
source: Examining the basic interactions between serotonin receptor-medicated second messenger systems and immune-related intracellular signaling pathways in insects may shed light on their interactions and functions in mammals.
evidence: Based on the relative simplicity of the insect immune system compared to mammals.

claim: Naive hemocytes express 5-HT1B, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT7 receptors, but only 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B appear to have functional roles.
source: Second, our findings show that naive hemocytes express 5-HT1B, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT7 receptors, but only 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B appear to have functional roles.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR, pharmacological, and RNAi data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Using selective antagonists and RNAi, inhibition of 5-HT1B decreases hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: Using selective antagonists and RNAi, we found that inhibition of 5-HT1B decreases hemocyte phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological and RNAi data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Inhibition of 5-HT2B enhances hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: However, inhibition of 5-HT2B enhances hemocyte phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological and RNAi data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Activation of 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B affects hemocytes in opposite ways.
source: It seems that activation of these two receptors affects hemocytes in opposite ways.
evidence: Inferred from the opposite effects of receptor blockade on phagocytosis.

claim: 5-HT1B is dramatically up-regulated following hemocyte activation.
source: Interestingly, we found that 5-HT1B is dramatically up-regulated following hemocyte activation, but 5-HT2B is significantly down-regulated.
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 5-HT2B is significantly down-regulated following hemocyte activation.
source: Interestingly, we found that 5-HT1B is dramatically up-regulated following hemocyte activation, but 5-HT2B is significantly down-regulated.
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The overall effects of 5-HT signaling induced by immune challenge are favorable for hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: Therefore, even though the two receptors have opposite functions upon activation, the overall effects of 5-HT signaling induced by immune challenge are favorable for hemocyte phagocytosis (Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from the differential regulation of receptors and the net effect of 5-HT on phagocytosis.

claim: Mammalian DCs express 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B, via which 5-HT induces chemotaxis and in vivo migration of DCs to draining lymph nodes.
source: Mammalian DCs also express 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B, via which 5-HT induces chemotaxis and in vivo migration of DCs to draining lymph nodes (Müller et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Müller et al., 2009.

claim: 5-HT activates macrophage cells via 5-HT1A.
source: Even though insect plasmatocytes are macrophage-like cells, 5-HT activates macrophage cells via 5-HT1A (Nakamura et al., 2008) and 5-HT2C (Mikulski et al., 2010), which are different from the receptor sub-types found in insect hemocytes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2008.

claim: 5-HT activates macrophage cells via 5-HT2C.
source: Even though insect plasmatocytes are macrophage-like cells, 5-HT activates macrophage cells via 5-HT1A (Nakamura et al., 2008) and 5-HT2C (Mikulski et al., 2010), which are different from the receptor sub-types found in insect hemocytes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mikulski et al., 2010.

claim: The 5-HT7 receptor plays a critical role in the immune response in the gut of mice.
source: The 5-HT7 receptor plays a critical role in the immune response in the gut of mice (Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013.

claim: 5-HT7 receptors were not involved in insect hemocyte phagocytosis.
source: Although our results indicated that 5-HT7 receptors were not involved in insect hemocyte phagocytosis, they may be critical for other immune activities.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological and RNAi data showing no effect of 5-HT7 blockade on phagocytosis.

claim: 5-HT7 receptors may be critical for other immune activities.
source: Although our results indicated that 5-HT7 receptors were not involved in insect hemocyte phagocytosis, they may be critical for other immune activities.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the expression of 5-HT7 in hemocytes despite lack of phagocytosis effect.

claim: Many neurotransmitter receptors are found on mammalian immune cells and regulate innate immune response.
source: Many neurotransmitter receptors are found on mammalian immune cells and regulate innate immune response, however, it is still unclear about their general role at the organismal level because most studies are conducted in vitro (Sternberg, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sternberg, 2006.

claim: It is still unclear about the general role of neurotransmitter receptors at the organismal level because most studies are conducted in vitro.
source: Many neurotransmitter receptors are found on mammalian immune cells and regulate innate immune response, however, it is still unclear about their general role at the organismal level because most studies are conducted in vitro (Sternberg, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sternberg, 2006 and general knowledge of the field.

claim: It is relatively easy to test immunity in insects in vivo.
source: However, it is relatively easy to test immunity in insects in vivo (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007.

claim: The 5-HT1B deficiency flies were more vulnerable to bacterial infections due to their poor phagocytic ability.
source: We found that the 5-HT1B deficiency flies were more vulnerable to bacterial infections due to their poor phagocytic ability.
evidence: Supported by survival, phagocytosis, and bacterial load data in Figure 6.

claim: Hemocyte-specific RNAi experiments showed similar results to 5-HT1B null mutants, indicating that the 5-HT1B-mediated hemocyte phagocytosis is important for insects to defend themselves against pathogens.
source: Hemocyte-specific RNAi experiments showed similar results, indicating that the 5-HT1B-mediated hemocyte phagocytosis is important for insects to defend themselves against pathogens.
evidence: Supported by hemocyte-specific RNAi data in Figure 7.

claim: The flies expressing 5-HT2B RNAi in their hemocytes were more susceptible to bacterial infections, suggesting that activation of 5-HT2B may promote phagocytosis in Drosophila, different from the results in P. rapae.
source: Surprisingly, the flies expressing 5-HT2B RNAi in their hemocytes were more susceptible to bacterial infections, suggesting that activation of 5-HT2B may promote phagocytosis in Drosophila, different from the results in P. rapae.
evidence: Supported by survival and phagocytosis data in Figure 8, contrasted with P. rapae results.

claim: Insect hemocytes can synthesis and release 5-HT, which regulates phagocytosis via 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors on the membrane of the hemocyte.
source: In conclusion, we found that insect hemocytes can synthesis and release 5-HT, which regulates phagocytosis via 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B receptors on the membrane of the hemocyte.
evidence: Supported by the combined experimental data from Figures 1-8.

claim: The genetic model Drosophila was used to further confirm the roles of 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B in vivo.
source: We also used the genetic model Drosophila to further confirm the roles of 5-HT1B and 5-HT2B in vivo.
evidence: Supported by Drosophila experiments in Figures 6-8.

claim: Serotonin, an ancient signaling molecule, modifies immune function in animals across phyla.
source: These findings suggest that serotonin, an ancient signaling molecule, modifies immune function in animals across phyla.
evidence: Inferred from the conservation of serotonergic immune modulation observed across insects and vertebrates.

claim: Exploring the interactions between serotonin receptor-mediated pathways and immune-related pathways may be easier to initiate in insects, which have a simpler immune system.
source: Exploring the interactions between serotonin receptor-mediated pathways and immune-related pathways may be easier to initiate in insects, which have a simpler immune system.
evidence: Based on the relative simplicity of the insect immune system compared to mammals.
